headings.text: How your certificate maps to groups
What this means for your integration

blocks.html:
Your certificate gets you in; your groups decide what you can do. On a Deploy App deployment, groups live in Keycloak and are relayed to TAK Server — so Keycloak is where access to TAK data is actually shaped.

Keycloak's two jobs

  1. OIDC identity provider. Keycloak is the OpenID Connect IdP for the deployment. TAK Server's OAuth API consumes it — the spec's OAuth endpoints (getOpenIdConfiguration, getAccessToken, handleAuthRequest, getAuthServerName) are how TAK Server discovers Keycloak's OIDC configuration and accepts tokens from it. This is what lets a Keycloak-authenticated user reach TAK Server without a separate login. Concretely, TAK Server runs the OAuth2 Password flow and exposes a token endpoint at **https://<server>:8446/oauth/token**, issuing JWTs signed by the server certificate (so external systems can validate them against the server's trust chain). Certificate auth uses port 8443; OAuth/username-password (incl. WebTAK) uses 8446.
  2. Group management. Keycloak is where a deployment's user groups are defined and assigned. "The current Deploy App environment uses Keycloak to manage user groups. These groups are relayed to TAK Server and connected users get them automatically."

Logging into Keycloak

Admins reach Keycloak with the mTLS certificate issued by RASENMAEHER (the same one from the previous page):

  • Open kc.<your-server> (e.g. kc.your-server.fi) and authenticate with the mTLS client certificate.
  • Go to Groups in the sidebar → the tak groups to manage TAK access.

How TAK Server groups work

TAK Server uses groups to decide who sees what — users in the same group share and view each other's information. Membership has a direction:

Membership Meaning Keycloak group
In the user sends (writes) data to the group <group>_WRITE
Out the user receives (reads) data from the group <group>_READ
Both the user both sends and receives <group>
  • Everyone starts in the default group; admins move users as needed, and a user can be in multiple groups.
  • Basic users don't see or change groups — group management is an admin task, visible through TAK tools and the TAK Server admin UI.

This direction model is why a push can silently go nowhere: to send into a group you need In (_WRITE) membership; to read it you need Out (_READ).

How your certificate maps to groups

TAK Server can assign a connection's groups three ways: from the input (a <filtergroup> on the listening port), from an authentication message (the client sends username/password), or from the client certificate (auth="x509"). The Deploy App path is the client-certificate one, and it works like this:

  1. You connect with your mTLS client certificate.
  2. TAK Server reads the CN from the certificate's DN and treats it as your username — e.g. CN=jkirk, O=TAK, C=US → username jkirk.
  3. It looks that username up in its authentication backend and applies the groups found there (the <group> / <group>_WRITE / <group>_READ memberships managed via Keycloak).
  4. If no groups are found, the connection lands in the default **__ANON__** group (two underscores each side).

So there's a clean chain: your Deploy App cert's CN → username → group lookup → the In/Out/Both memberships Keycloak manages. Changing your groups in Keycloak changes what that certificate can see and send on TAK Server — no new certificate required.

What this means for your integration

  • The certificate identity you enrolled is subject to the same group rules as any user. Put your integration's identity in the right groups (In/Out/Both) for the data it must send and receive.
  • Need your bridge to publish to a team? Give it In on that group. Need it to ingest a team's traffic? Give it Out. A two-way relay needs Both.
  • Changing a user's (or service's) TAK visibility is done in Keycloak, not on TAK Server directly — the change is relayed automatically.
